Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
217 AM EDT Tue Sep 8 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 216 AM EDT Tuesday...

Forecast precipitation amounts have increased slightly for the 
Wednesday into Thursday morning system, and the arrival of 
precipitation continues to trend earlier in the day Wednesday than 
the previous forecast.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 216 AM EDT Tuesday...

1. Mostly dry and seasonable weather is expected today and 
tonight, then more widespread precipitation arrives Wednesday into 
Wednesday night.

2. High pressure will bring another stretch of dry and pleasant 
weather to start the weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 216 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A dying cold front will come through early this morning 
and bring a few light showers, but weak forcing and dry low levels 
will minimize the impacts. Ridging will become more established and 
dominate the synoptic pattern going into Wednesday, continuing the 
quiet and relatively seasonable to above normal stretch. Overall, 
highs will be in the 70s to lower 80s through Thursday. Lows tonight 
will be in the mid 40s to lower 60s, increasing to the upper 50s to 
mid 60s Wednesday night with the arrival of a warm frontal boundary 
attached to a deepening low pressure system in Canada. While warm 
air advection will bring a more humid airmass into the region, there 
will not be enough time for a fully tropical airmass to become 
established. Rain arrives throughout the day Wednesday in northern 
areas as a warm front pushes through, though it appears to lack much 
elevated instability, so the rain should just be stratiform. The 
center of the low will pass by well to the north of our area, and 
the best dynamics should miss the region. Therefore, this will limit 
instability as the system passes by. The highest instability will be 
across the St. Lawrence Valley where the warmer airmass has the most 
time to become established. Dew points there should briefly reach 
the mid 60s to around 70 and a few rumbles of thunder are possible 
there. The cold front passes through Wednesday night into early 
Thursday, but the warm sector never looks to become fully 
established in the region, so most convection should remain to the 
southwest. St. Lawrence County and southern Vermont look to be the 
places that may see more convective enhancement, while the rest of 
the region should mostly see synoptically forced rain. However, if 
the trend of earlier precipitation and a faster system continues, we 
may see more availability of instability on Wednesday for more 
widespread thunderstorms. A strong southwesterly low-level jet will 
reach the 40-55 KT range at 850 mb Wednesday and Wednesday night, 
causing downsloping in the typical spots like the Champlain Valley, 
which could limit rainfall totals. Overall expected totals range in 
the 0.15 to 0.75 inch range for most places, with some higher totals 
locally along the spine of the Green Mountains and Adirondacks. This 
jet will also lead to widespread gusts in the 20-30 mph range, with 
locally higher gusts, particularly on summits. Then Thursday, winds 
should stay elevated in cold air advection out of the west and 
northwest.

KEY MESSAGE 2: High pressure will build into the region towards the end 
of the week into the weekend, bringing a stretch of dry and pleasant 
weather. Daytime high temperatures on Friday will generally be in 
the upper 60s and low 70s, with warmer temperatures expected for 
Saturday and Sunday in the 70s to near 80 as the ridging shifts 
eastward leading to southerly flow across the region. Ideal 
radiational cooling conditions are expected, especially Friday night 
into Saturday morning with the high pressure overhead. Overnight 
lows are expected to drop into the 40s, with some of the cold 
hollows dropping into the mid/upper 30s while locations near Lake 
Champlain will stay in the 50s. While dry weather will persist 
through much of the weekend, precipitation chances will increase 
through the day on Sunday with a shortwave trough pushing through, 
although there is still plenty of uncertainty regarding this feature.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Through 06Z Wednesday...VFR conditions currently prevail across
all terminals, with a weak cold front expected to drop across
the region later this morning, bringing some chances for lower
ceilings and chances for light rain showers. Northern terminals
(KEFK,KSLK,KBTV,KMSS) have the best chances of seeing some MVFR
ceilings develop towards sunrise, with some IFR potential at 
KEFK. Winds look to be strong enough to prevent any fog 
development. Lower ceilings will linger through the morning, 
with all terminals expected to return towards VFR by the 
afternoon. Winds will be continue to be light and terrain driven
(with stronger SE drainage wind at KRUT) for the next few 
hours, trending north to northwest through the day tomorrow 
generally remaining less than 10 knots.

Outlook...

Wednesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Wednesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Definite
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Thursday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&
